Fall here means September–November. This synopsis is being written as the season unfolds; later parts will cover the season's temperature and precipitation against normal, its events, and the atmospheric pattern.

## Part 1: Warm water off Baja California

Sea-surface temperatures off Baja California were the highest in the ERSSTv5 record since 1950 for each of July, August and September 2026. Averaged over 18–32°N, 122–108°W (the Pacific side of the peninsula and the Gulf of California), the anomaly relative to 1991–2020 was +1.81 °C in July, +1.90 °C in August, +2.15 °C in September. The previous September record was +1.43 °C in 2015. Over the same period Flagstaff had its two largest rain events of the autumn, [September 27–30](../events/2026-09-27.qmd) and [October 9–13](../events/2026-10-09.qmd). National Weather Service forecasters in Flagstaff attributed the moisture in both to eastern Pacific tropical cyclones: in late September first the remnants of Odalys and then Polo, and in October Rachel (see [What the forecasters said](#what-the-forecasters-said)). The airport recorded 8.89 in from September 1 through October 22, already the 2nd largest September–October total of 76 years since 1950.

### Sea-surface temperature under the storm tracks

| Storm   | Time (UTC)   | Position       | Status         |   Wind (kt) |   SST (°C) |   1991–2020 normal (°C) |   Difference (°C) | SST month   |
|:--------|:-------------|:---------------|:---------------|------------:|-----------:|------------------------:|------------------:|:------------|
| Polo    | Sep 28 12:00 | 23.9°N 113.7°W | hurricane      |         100 |       28.3 |                    25.2 |               3   | Sep         |
| Polo    | Sep 29 00:00 | 25.2°N 112.8°W | hurricane      |         100 |       30.4 |                    27.7 |               2.7 | Sep         |
| Polo    | Sep 29 12:00 | 26.9°N 111.6°W | hurricane      |          65 |       30.4 |                    27.7 |               2.7 | Sep         |
| Rachel  | Oct 10 00:00 | 23.3°N 123.6°W | tropical storm |          40 |       24.3 |                    23   |               1.3 | Sep         |
| Rachel  | Oct 10 12:00 | 24.7°N 120.5°W | tropical storm |          50 |       25.5 |                    23.5 |               2   | Sep         |
| Rachel  | Oct 11 00:00 | 28.5°N 117.0°W | tropical storm |          55 |       24.6 |                    21.4 |               3.1 | Sep         |

The table lists 12-hourly positions north of 23°N over water. Along them, SST was 24.3–30.4 °C, +1.3 to +3.1 °C relative to normal. Values are monthly means at the nearest 2° ERSSTv5 cell; October positions use September SST, the latest month available.


Sea-surface temperatures of about 26 °C or more are generally needed to sustain a tropical cyclone. On the Pacific side of the peninsula, the northernmost September SST of at least 26 °C was at 22°N along 120°W (normal 18°N); 24°N along 118°W (normal 20°N); 26°N along 116°W (normal 20°N) (solid and dashed contours above). The Gulf of California normally exceeds 26 °C in September.


Polo was still a 100-kt hurricane at 25°N and a hurricane at 27°N before dissipating over Sonora; Rachel was still a tropical storm at 28.5°N, and its remnant reached southeastern California.

Warm water does not steer storms. In both events a trough west of California turned the moisture plume toward Arizona; see the atmospheric setting on the [September 27–30](../events/2026-09-27.qmd) and [October 9–13](../events/2026-10-09.qmd) pages.

### What the forecasters said

The National Weather Service office in Flagstaff discussed the moisture source in its Area Forecast Discussions as the event unfolded. Excerpts, quoted verbatim (links to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive):

- **Sep 24, 10:16 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609250516)): "Moisture associated with two tropical cyclones (Hurricane Polo forecast to be off the southern Baja at this time and TS Odalys much farther west) will be pulled northeastward into the southwest United States in advance of this trough."
- **Sep 26, 1:23 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609262023)): "Despite the fact the tropical moisture is coming from two tropical cyclones to the south, neither one of these circulations will actually make it up into Arizona."
- **Sep 28, 11:43 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609281843)): "Current satellite imagery show a plume of moisture originating from the remnants of Odalys moving across northern Arizona. Meanwhile, Hurricane Polo is centered of the west coast of Southern Baja California."
- **Sep 29, 2:03 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609292103)): "Arizona remains under a very dynamic weather pattern today with upper level low pressure centered over western Arizona and moisture from Hurricane Polo streaming northward."
- **Sep 30, 2:12 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609300912)): "Water vapor satellite imagery show the upper-level low pressure centered over central Arizona and moving eastward, with moisture from the remnants of Polo now mostly being lifted into eastern New Mexico and western Texas."
- **Oct 8, 2:42 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610080942)): "As the trough digs south, it will interact with what will become the remnants of TS Rachel."
- **Oct 10, 10:48 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610101748)): "Tropical Storm Rachel, about 500 miles southwest of San Diego as of 8 AM MST, is quickly moving northward as it begins to be pulled northward by an upper-level low off the California coast."
- **Oct 11, 3:01 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610111001)): "After making landfall earlier this evening, the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel are moving towards the north- northeast early this morning before exiting into Utah this afternoon. … With a continued strong southerly flow, moisture has continued to advect into the region and have left ripe conditions with the potential for heavy rain through today."
- **Oct 11, 11:25 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610111825)): "Moisture from Hurricane Rachel has moved into much of northern Arizona this morning, with PWAT values near or exceeding daily record levels."


The forecasters' account matches the ERA5 analysis on the event pages. In the September event, the first surge of moisture was traced by the forecasters to the remnants of Odalys, which stayed west of 123°W and south of 23°N, outside the Baja box; at the time of peak moisture transport over Flagstaff (September 28) ERA5 shows no continuous plume back to Polo. Polo's moisture followed on September 29 as the upper-level low crossed Arizona. In the October event, ERA5 shows the plume over Flagstaff continuous with Rachel at the time of peak moisture transport, and the forecasters reported precipitable water near or above daily records.


### Has warm water off Baja meant a wet autumn before?

::: {#dd2f6ae6 .cell execution_count=9}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![September SST anomaly in the Baja box against Flagstaff airport September–October precipitation, 1950–2025, with a least-squares line. 2026 (orange) uses precipitation reported so far.](fall-2026_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){}
:::
:::


- **Correlation, 1950–2025 (n = 76):** r = +0.22 (p = 0.05) between September Baja SST anomaly and Flagstaff September–October precipitation. For comparison, July–September ONI gives r = +0.25.
- **Overlap with ENSO:** the Baja box correlates with July–September ONI at r = +0.50. With ONI removed from both, the Baja–precipitation correlation is +0.12 (p = 0.31).
- **Warmest fifth of Septembers (n = 16):** 10 were followed by above-median September–October precipitation; their median was 3.65 in, against 3.23 in for all years. The driest of them was 2020, the 3rd warmest September, with 0.05 in.


In the record, warm water off Baja has gone with modestly wetter autumns in Flagstaff, and much of that relationship is shared with El Niño. On its own it has not been enough: a wet autumn also needs storms in the eastern Pacific and a pattern that brings their moisture north.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Notes and caveats

- **Baseline:** anomalies are relative to 1991–2020. Long-term warming raises recent anomalies relative to earlier decades, so part of 2026's margin over earlier years reflects the trend; 2026 also exceeds the recent record years.
- **Resolution:** ERSSTv5 is a 2°, monthly reconstruction. It does not resolve the narrow coastal upwelling zone or day-to-day changes under a storm.
- **Precipitation:** Flagstaff airport, threaded station record from RCC-ACIS. The 2026 value is incomplete until October ends.
- **Storm tracks:** NHC operational best-track files; final tracks are issued after the season.
:::
